    "response": "# Erdős #99 — Adversarial analysis of oblique lattices

Verdict: OPEN. I obtain a rigorous global-comparison theorem excluding fixed-angle oblique-lattice configurations as exact minimizers for sufficiently large cardinality. I also obtain an explicit family of arbitrarily large triangle-free oblique-lattice configurations for which no phase-angle deformation can reduce the diameter. This provides a counterexample to an otherwise tempting relaxation argument.

Neither result settles the original conjecture. In particular, the phase-angle obstruction does not establish global optimality, and the global-comparison theorem does not cover angles converging to 60∘60^\circ60∘ sufficiently rapidly.

The distinction between these two results is important: a configuration can be locally and even globally optimal within a prescribed lattice-deformation family while being strictly worse than the unrestricted global optimum.

### What this theorem actually establishes

There are several important strengths.

- It covers arbitrary finite subsets of the oblique lattice.
- It includes all boundary geometries and all possible active-pair patterns.
- It compares against an actual nnn-point feasible competitor, not merely an asymptotic density.
- It establishes strict non-globality, not just a difference in limiting packing densities.

It is consequently stronger than an argument that merely observes that the oblique lattice has lower bulk density.

However, it does not exclude a sequence of lattices with

θn⟶π3.\theta_n\longrightarrow\frac{\pi}{3}.θn​⟶3π​.

The positive area gap then disappears, and the error terms in the finite-cardinality inequalities become relevant.

That is a substantial remaining gap.

This is a useful distinction:

The phase-angle obstruction is therefore real, but it is not a global counterexample.

## 5. The general phase-angle criterion

The construction suggests a useful exact formulation for any finite lattice patch.

For a fixed finite coordinate set S⊂Z2S\subset\mathbb Z^2S⊂Z2, define

FS(c)=diam⁡(S;θ)2,c=cos⁡θ.F_S(c)= \operatorname{diam}(S;\theta)^2, \qquad c=\cos\theta.FS​(c)=diam(S;θ)2,c=cosθ.

This function is the maximum of finitely many affine functions. Hence it is convex and piecewise linear.

A convex function has an interior minimum precisely when its left derivative is nonpositive and its right derivative is nonnegative.

## 6. What kind of stability theorem could actually activate a contact?

There is a useful distinction between ordinary metric stability and exact finite rigidity.

Metric stability says that a configuration close to an extremal crystalline arrangement has distances close to the corresponding crystalline distances.

Exact finite rigidity says that the configuration cannot move at all while satisfying the relevant constraints.

The second is substantially stronger.

### 6.3 Why it does not solve Erdős #99

There are three missing ingredients.

First, the crystalline limit is not a finite exact reference configuration. Its unit edges need not be exact unit edges in the approximating original configurations.

Second, the original diameter constraint does not automatically pin every diametral endpoint pointwise. A perturbation can shorten a diametral pair while preserving the upper diameter bound.

Third, even a locally isolated finite framework need not contain a triangle.

The rhombic lattice illustrates the last point: it has exact unit contacts and no unit triangle. A boundary can pin a finite rhombic framework at an angle strictly greater than 60∘60^\circ60∘. Local rigidity at that angle would not turn its short diagonal into a unit distance.

The useful conclusion is therefore conditional:

> If one can exhibit an exact finite globally optimal reference framework, prove that its diametral boundary anchors are uniquely pinned, and establish anchored cone rigidity, then nearby exact optimizers can be forced to coincide with that reference framework.

But if the reference framework is rhombic and K3-free, the conclusion is K3-free, not triangular.

To prove Erdős #99, one additionally needs an argument that the globally selected finite framework has at least one exact 60∘60^\circ60∘ rhombic angle or another original unit-triangle mechanism.

That is the unresolved activation step.

The useful published result is the expansive-motion theorem of Robert Connelly, Erik D. Demaine, and Günter Rote (CDR), Straightening Polygonal Arcs and Convexifying Polygonal Cycles, Discrete & Computational Geometry 30 (2003), 205–239.

Lemma (path-cover contact opening). Suppose a finite set of triangular-lattice vertices is partitioned into vertex-disjoint, noncrossing polygonal paths whose edges are unit lattice edges. There are arbitrarily small perturbations preserving every selected path edge at length exactly 111, strictly increasing every other initially unit pair distance, and not decreasing any pair distance.

Justification. Apply the CDR expansive motion to the collection of open paths. Its strictness statement excludes pairs joined by straight bar subchains. Distinct endpoints of a straight subchain of two or more unit bars are separated by at least 222, so such a pair cannot be an unselected unit contact. Consequently every unselected unit pair strictly separates. Already longer distances remain at least their original values. Continuity permits an arbitrarily small displacement.

Thus the complete unit-contact graph after perturbation is exactly the selected path cover, rather than merely containing that cover. This assertion applies to finite planar path linkages, not general branching trees or arbitrary contact subgraphs. UserPages

The focused literature yields a useful distinction.

Planar equilateral trees can be locked as noncrossing bar linkages. The explicit seven-arm example is nevertheless excluded from unit-separated contact graphs by a degree obstruction. Prestress stability, unlike KKT equilibrium or linkage locking, provides a rigorous sufficient certificate for strict ordinary diameter-local minimality, even when the contact graph is a tree.

The strongest directly applicable finite tools established here are the forest cut identity (2), the quadratic sufficiency test (3), and the rigid-branch hinge descent lemma.

What remains unproved is the decisive alternative: either establish a diameter-decreasing feasible motion for every sufficiently large unit-separated forest-contact candidate, or produce an admissible large forest construction together with an exact local-minimality certificate.

In particular, there is no demonstrated positive-definite prestress certificate for an unbounded family of such trees, no applicable universal spider-unfolding theorem, and no justification for upgrading near-round geometry, optimal leading density, or positive KKT multipliers to ordinary local or global optimality.
